definition: Not widely known or noticed by most people.
example: Her thesis focused on an obscure poet who published only one small book of verse.
nuance: Obscure means known to few, not to none; unlike unknown, it can also describe writing or meaning that is hard to understand.
prompt: A music fan describes a band she discovered in a tiny secondhand record shop.
options: The band was so obscure that its only album sold a few hundred copies.
The obscure band's hit single played on nearly every radio station in the country.
The obscure lyrics were so rude that the shop owner refused to play them aloud.
Fans everywhere recognized the band's obscure guitar sound within a single note.
reasons: Selling to just a few hundred listeners shows that hardly anyone has heard of the band.
Airplay on almost every station would make a band famous, the reverse of little-known.
This confuses the word with obscene; rudeness has nothing to do with being little-known.
A sound that fans everywhere instantly recognize is famous, not something few people know.

practice.prompt: A student is choosing a person to research for a history report.
options: She called the inventor obscure because he cheated his business partners.
She chose an obscure inventor whose name appears in just a few old newspapers.
She chose an obscure inventor whose face is printed on the national currency.
Research was easy because every textbook covers the obscure inventor at great length.
reasons: Dishonesty is a moral failing; it says nothing about how few people know a person.
Showing up in only a handful of old sources marks someone history has mostly overlooked.
A person pictured on money that everyone handles is about as well known as anyone can be.
Thorough coverage in every textbook means the inventor is widely known and well documented.
